current_state_summary: War ongoing, no armistice, at historically low territorial exchange rates. Net Russian gain June 16-July 14 2026 was 5 sq mi (ISW) to 15 sq mi (DeepState) over four weeks; prior four weeks 10 sq mi. Russia took Pokrovsk/Myrnohrad in early 2026 (entered Nov 2025) but has not exploited west of it since Dec 2025; the Kramatorsk-Kostiantynivka belt is now the main Russian axis. Ukraine's Feb-Mar 2026 Oleksandrivka/southern counteroffensive retook ~300-400 km2 and cleared eight settlements, effectively clearing Dnipropetrovsk oblast and halting Russia's Dnepr grouping near Orikhiv. Attrition: ~1.4m cumulative Russian casualties Feb 2022-June 2026, 400-450k fatalities; 2026 running 30-34k casualties/month vs ~27k recruits/month (940/day actual vs 1,100-1,150 target); March 2026 set a single-month record of 35,000. Losses have exceeded intake for every month since Dec 2025. Ukraine faces its own manpower crisis: target end-2026 force 850k, 165,200 AWOL criminal cases in the first 10 months of 2025, 80k+ total deserters; June 2026 mobilisation reform package announced. Diplomacy: Geneva trilateral Feb 17-18 2026 was the first round to put territory on the agenda; a US-set June 2026 deadline lapsed; Zelensky's June 4 letter proposing a leaders' meeting was rebuffed by Putin, who insists on full Donbas. Only two truces held, both short humanitarian pauses (32-hour Orthodox Easter truce from 11 April 2026; 9-11 May Victory Day truce). As of 26-28 July 2026 Washington and Kyiv are drafting an 'air ceasefire' (halt to long-range strikes) to put to Moscow; Peskov calls comment premature; Zelensky meets Trump in Washington this week. US mediation has been partly displaced by the Iran war. Deep-strike campaign: Ukraine has hit all ten of Russia's largest refineries in 2026 (11 refineries struck in June alone), disabling 42.7% of projected refining capacity as of early July, cutting ~500 kb/d of crude runs; cumulative refining-sector losses ~$13.5bn since Aug 2025; fuel rationing and export bans inside Russia. Russian economy: CBR July 2026 GDP forecast cut to 0.0-1.0%; key rate cut 25bp to 14.00% on 24 July (from 21% peak, via 15% and 14.5% in April); CPI 6.0% y/y in June, CBR 2026 range 6-7%; Jan-Apr 2026 federal deficit $78.4bn against a $50.5bn full-year plan; hydrocarbon revenue -38.3% to $30.6bn Jan-Apr; NWF liquid assets $35.7bn (vs $185bn in 2021); 2026 spending 44.1tn RUB = 18.7% of GDP; MoD outlays reached 7.3% of GDP in 2025. Urals $54.28/bbl (28 July), ~$7 discount to Brent at Indian ports; EU price cap frozen at $44.10 by the 21st sanctions package agreed 23 July 2026. EU immobilised €210bn of Russian assets indefinitely in Dec 2025 but Belgium blocked the reparations loan; leaders instead agreed a €90bn EU-borrowed loan for 2026-27. NATO's Ankara summit (7-8 July 2026) named Russia a threat, pledged €70bn of military aid for 2026 with equivalent intent for 2027, and logged >$139bn of added European/Canadian core defence investment since The Hague. European allies plus Canada budget ~$634bn in 2026 = 2.53% of GDP (EU-27 alone €454bn, up from €418bn, = 2.4% of EU GDP) against the 3.5%-core/5%-total-by-2035 target; Lithuania 5.33%, Estonia 5.1%, Latvia 4.92%; Spain still refuses 5%. Countervailing: Hegseth has cut US fighters in Europe 150->100, tankers by 8, ISR 26->15, BCTs 4->3, cancelled a 4,000-strong Poland/Romania rotation, is pulling ~5,000 troops from Germany, and left ~1,000 in Romania. Politics: Orban lost on 12 April 2026 - Magyar's Tisza took 53.6% and 138/199 seats on ~80% turnout; the new government ended Hungary's 17-month veto, cluster 1 of Ukraine/Moldova accession opened 15 June, but Budapest still blocked clusters 2-3 on 22 July (next attempt 1 September). Germany: Merz's CDU/CSU-SPD coalition agreed a reform package 1-2 July, but AfD hit a record 28-29% (Insa 29%, 8.5pt lead over CDU/CSU at ~22%) ahead of September eastern state elections. France remains in budgetary paralysis under a Lecornu minority government. Hybrid pressure: Romania logged 7 drone airspace violations, 11 munition-fragment finds and 18 air-policing scrambles by 28 April, then shot down drones on three consecutive days in late July (its first-ever kinetic engagements); NATO downed a drone over Latvia on 8 June. Operation Eastern Sentry and Baltic Sentry continue. Periphery: Armenia-Azerbaijan treaty initialled Aug 2025 but unsigned pending Armenian constitutional change, with Pashinyan re-legitimised by 7 June 2026 elections and US-managed TRIPP corridor displacing Russia; Georgia's candidacy frozen amid authoritarian consolidation; Belarus hosts Oreshnik and rehearsed non-strategic nuclear employment with Russia in May 2026.

indicators.label: Russia-NATO tension composite (0-100)
indicators.source: GEO-SIM composite of NATO air-policing scrambles, Article 4 invocations, attributed airspace violations, and ISW/RUSI/Institut Montaigne escalation assessments. Anchors: 2013=25, 2014=45, Feb-Mar 2022=90, 2024=62, Sept 2025 (Poland/Estonia Art.4)=74.

indicators.label: Ukraine war intensity composite (0-100)
indicators.source: GEO-SIM composite of combined monthly casualties, long-range strike/drone sortie volume and monthly territorial change. Anchors: Mar 2022=100, 2023 (Bakhmut/counteroffensive)=82, 2024=78, 2025=80, H1 2026=73 (record casualty rates but near-zero manoeuvre).

indicators.label: NATO European allies + Canada core defence spending, % of GDP
indicators.source: NATO defence expenditure estimates via ICDS 'Defence Spending: Who Is Doing What' (July 2026) and NATO def-exp tables: ~$634bn = 2.53% of combined GDP in 2026, up from 2.02% (2024) and ~2.2% (2025). EU-27 alone: €454bn = 2.4% (2026) vs €418bn (2025).

indicators.label: Russian war-economy stress composite (0-100)
indicators.source: GEO-SIM composite of federal deficit/GDP, NWF liquid depletion rate, oil&gas revenue y/y, CPI, key rate and refinery outage share. Anchors: 2019=25, Mar 2022=72, 2023=45, 2024=40, 2025=55. Inputs: Bank of Russia, MinFin, OSW, Bank of Finland BOFIT, Moscow Times.

indicators.label: Western/Central European political fragmentation composite (0-100)
indicators.source: GEO-SIM composite of effective number of parliamentary parties, national-populist vote share, and government-formation duration across DE/FR/IT/ES/NL/PL/SE/CZ/AT/BE. Anchors: 2005=35, 2015=45, 2019=52, 2024=59. Inputs: PopuList, PolitPro, ECFR.

indicators.label: Urals crude export price
indicators.source: Urals spot quotes (oilpriceapi/TankerMap/Argus-derived); $54.28 on 28 July 2026, ~$7 discount to Brent at Indian ports. Dec 2025 monthly average ~$39; 2026 Russian budget assumed $59; EU price cap frozen at $44.10 (21st package, 23 July 2026).

indicators.label: Bank of Russia key policy rate
indicators.source: Bank of Russia press release, 24 July 2026: -25bp to 14.00%. Path: 21.0% (Oct 2024-May 2025 peak) -> 17% (Sept 2025) -> 15% -> 14.5% (April 2026) -> 14.0%.

indicators.label: Russian federal budget deficit, % of GDP
indicators.source: Russian MinFin monthly execution; Jan-Apr 2026 deficit $78.4bn vs $50.5bn planned for the full year; hydrocarbon revenue -38.3% y/y. History: 2020 3.8%, 2021 +0.4%, 2022 2.3%, 2023 1.9%, 2024 1.7%, 2025 ~2.6%.

indicators.label: National Wealth Fund liquid assets
indicators.source: Russian MinFin / Moscow Times / OSW; $185bn (2021) -> $35.7bn (mid-2026); some estimates put the liquid portion at $48.4bn. Record daily FX/gold sales of RUB 12.8bn/day ran 16 Jan-5 Feb 2026.

indicators.label: Russian killed+wounded+missing per month
indicators.source: CSIS 'Russian Blood and Treasure' and Ukrainian General Staff / Mediazona-Meduza reconciliation: 30,000-34,000/month in 2026, record 35,000 in March 2026; ~1.4m cumulative and 400-450k fatalities Feb 2022-June 2026. History: 2022 ~15k/mo, 2023 ~22k/mo, 2024 ~30k/mo.

indicators.label: Share of Ukraine's 1991 territory under Russian control
indicators.source: ISW/DeepState mapping via Russia Matters War Report Card. ~114,000 km2 of 603,550 km2. Net Russian change is now ~13-39 km2/month (5-15 sq mi per 4 weeks), i.e. ~0.03-0.08%/year; Ukraine reclaimed ~400 km2 in Dnipropetrovsk in Feb-Mar 2026.

indicators.label: US military personnel stationed/deployed in Europe
indicators.source: USEUCOM/DoD manpower data and press reporting on the 2026 posture review: ~100-105k peak (2022), ~80k (2024-25), ~72k mid-2026 with ~5,000 leaving Germany, BCTs cut 4->3, a 4,000-strong Poland/Romania rotation cancelled and ~1,000 retained in Romania. Pre-2022 baseline ~63-65k.

indicators.label: Attributed Russian airspace violations of NATO members per year
indicators.source: National MoD statements aggregated (Romania: 7 violations, 11 munition-fragment finds, 18 air-policing scrambles by 28 Apr 2026, then 3 shootdowns in 3 days late July; Poland Sept 2025 mass drone incursion; Estonia MiG-31 incursion Sept 2025; Latvia shootdown 8 June 2026). Pre-2022 run rate ~5-10/yr.

indicators.label: Attributed Russian sabotage/hybrid incidents in Europe per year
indicators.source: IISS/CSIS/Carnegie counts of arson, GPS jamming, parcel-IED, rail and subsea-cable sabotage: ~10 (2022), ~25 (2023), ~44 (2024), ~60-70 (2025-26). 11 Baltic subsea incidents by end-2025; NATO Baltic Sentry running since Jan 2025.

indicators.label: EU cohesion on Russia/Ukraine policy (0-100)
indicators.source: GEO-SIM composite of sanctions-renewal friction, enlargement-cluster progress, and joint-financing outcomes. 2026 inputs: 21st sanctions package adopted 23 July; Orban's defeat removed the main veto player; Hungary still blocked clusters 2-3 on 22 July; Belgium blocked the reparations loan (Dec 2025), forcing €90bn of EU-borrowed debt instead. Anchors: 2022=70, 2023=62, 2024=54, 2025=50.

indicators.label: Annualised external military + budget support to Ukraine
indicators.source: NATO Ankara summit declaration (€70bn military for 2026, equivalent intent for 2027) plus EU's €90bn 2026-27 loan facility (~€45bn/yr) plus residual bilateral; Kiel Institute tracker methodology. US direct appropriations now ~zero; PURL routes European purchases of US kit.

events.statement: A general ceasefire or armistice covering the entire Russia-Ukraine front takes effect and holds for at least 180 consecutive days.
events.resolution_criteria: A ceasefire/armistice agreed by both the Russian and Ukrainian governments (or imposed and observed de facto) covering all land, air and sea domains along the whole front, which OSCE/UN/ISW/ACLED reporting shows was not materially breached for 180 consecutive days. Local, seasonal, holiday, domain-limited (e.g. energy-only or air-only) or unilateral pauses do NOT count. Resolves YES on the 180th day.
events.reference_class: Interstate and internationalised wars lasting >4 years, Correlates of War / UCDP termination data: conditional annual war-termination hazard for wars already 4+ years old is roughly 15-20% (e.g. Iran-Iraq 8y, Korea 3y, Ethiopia-Eritrea 2y, Nagorno-Karabakh I 6y). Zero durable ceasefires in this war in 4.5 years despite 18 months of intensive US mediation, three summit-level attempts, and two announced humanitarian truces (April and May 2026), both under 72 hours.
events.reasoning: Outside view: wars of this age terminate at ~16%/yr. Adjustment upward for genuine exhaustion on both sides (Russian losses 30-34k/mo exceeding ~27k/mo recruitment for eight straight months; Ukrainian AWOL cases of 165,200 in ten months of 2025; 64% of Russians and 66% of Ukrainians favour negotiating now; Urals at $54 with the NWF down to $35.7bn) is largely offset by the specific evidence of failure: the June 2026 US deadline lapsed, Putin's public precondition is still full Donbas, and the live proposal on 26 July is only an *air* ceasefire, which would explicitly not resolve this. Net multiplier 1.15 -> hazard ~0.184/yr. Because 180 days of holding is required, the p_by_2027 window for a start date is only ~0.9yr: 1-exp(-0.184*0.9)=0.153 -> 0.16. p_by_2030 uses ~3.9 effective years: 1-exp(-0.184*3.9)=0.51 -> shaded to 0.49 since a partial/air-only settlement is a competing outcome that would satisfy neither side's need for a general ceasefire. p_by_2036: 1-exp(-0.184*9.9)=0.84, shaded to 0.79 for the frozen-conflict-without-formal-ceasefire path (the Korean and Donbas 2015-2022 precedents), where fighting decays below intensity thresholds but no instrument is signed.

events.statement: Russian forces achieve an operational breakthrough: capture of a Ukrainian oblast capital west of the current line (Zaporizhzhia city, Kharkiv, Dnipro, Sumy, Kherson) or the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration, or an advance of >50 km along a >40 km frontage within any 90-day window.
events.resolution_criteria: ISW and DeepState both assess Russian control of the built-up area of one of the named cities/agglomerations, OR both assess a net Russian advance of >50 km depth across a contiguous >40 km frontage within 90 days. Encirclement without control does not count.
events.reference_class: Manoeuvre breakthroughs in this war: three in 4.5 years (Russian Feb-Mar 2022, Ukrainian Kharkiv Sept 2022, Kherson withdrawal Nov 2022), all in the first year. Russian-initiated breakthroughs since March 2022: zero in 4.3 years. Broader class of positional attrition wars (WWI Western Front 1915-17, Iran-Iraq 1984-88, Korea 1951-53): operational breakthrough after positional stalemate sets in occurs at roughly 5-10%/yr, usually driven by one side's political or logistical collapse rather than by manoeuvre.
events.reasoning: Outside view 0.09/yr. Current conditions cut both ways and net to only 1.1x. Against: Russian net gains are running at 13-39 km2/month, the lowest sustained rate of the war; Russia failed to exploit Pokrovsk for eight months; casualties exceed recruitment; Ukraine executed a successful 400 km2 counteroffensive in Feb-Mar 2026 and halted the Dnepr grouping. For: Ukraine's infantry crisis is the single most plausible collapse mechanism, and US direct appropriations are now zero with PURL depending on European purchasing. Hazard ~0.10/yr while the war is active. Cumulative must be discounted by the probability the war is still active: expected war-active years are ~1.35 to end-2027, ~3.1 to 2030, ~5.0 to 2036 given the ceasefire hazard above. So p_2027 = 1-exp(-0.10*1.35) = 0.127 -> 0.12; p_2030 = 1-exp(-0.10*3.1) = 0.27 -> 0.26; p_2036 = 1-exp(-0.10*5.0) = 0.39, shaded to 0.34 because a breakthrough becomes progressively less likely the longer both armies remain drone-saturated (transparent battlefields structurally favour the defence).

events.statement: A direct exchange of fire between Russian state forces and the forces of a NATO member state causes at least one death on either side.
events.resolution_criteria: At least one fatality of a Russian serviceman/state operative or a NATO-member serviceman/civilian resulting from deliberate fire exchanged directly between Russian state forces and NATO-member forces, acknowledged by at least one of the two governments or established by NATO. Excludes: Russian forces killing NATO-member nationals fighting inside Ukraine as volunteers; drone/UAV shootdowns with no human casualty; accidents; sabotage without an exchange of fire.
events.reference_class: Direct lethal NATO-member vs Soviet/Russian engagements since 1945: a Cold War cluster in the 1950s (multiple US reconnaissance aircraft shot down, dozens of deaths, last major case RB-47 in 1960), then a 31-year gap, then Turkey's shootdown of a Russian Su-24 on 24 Nov 2015 (pilot killed). Post-1991: one instance in 35 years = 0.029/yr. Adding the near-miss set (Deir ez-Zor Feb 2018 against Wagner contractors; the Nov 2022 Przewodow missile impact killing two Poles, attributed to a Ukrainian air-defence round) gives ~0.04/yr.
events.reasoning: 2.6x is defensible and deliberately below the 5-10x that current coverage implies. The contact rate is genuinely unprecedented for the post-Cold-War period: Romania alone logged 7 airspace violations, 11 munition-fragment finds and 18 scrambles in four months, then engaged kinetically on three consecutive days in late July, and NATO downed a drone over Latvia on 8 June. Crucially, though, every 2026 engagement so far has been against unmanned systems, which cannot produce a fatality; the resolution bar requires manned engagement or a strike on NATO soil. Countervailing: NATO's rules of engagement have been tuned to avoid manned intercepts, Russia has consistently used deniable platforms precisely to stay below the lethal threshold, and Washington under this administration is an active brake. 0.04*2.6 = 0.104/yr while the war runs, decaying to ~0.035/yr afterwards. p_2027 = 1-exp(-0.104*1.4) = 0.135 -> 0.12 (shaded because most exposure is unmanned). p_2030 = 1-exp(-[0.104*2.6 + 0.035*1.8]) = 0.29 -> 0.27. p_2036 = 1-exp(-[0.33 + 0.21]) = 0.42 -> 0.38.

events.statement: NATO formally invokes Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty in response to a Russian action against a member state.
events.resolution_criteria: The North Atlantic Council adopts a decision explicitly invoking Article 5, naming Russia (or an unattributed armed attack widely attributed to Russia) as the source of the armed attack, confirmed by an official NATO statement.
events.reference_class: Article 5 has been invoked once in NATO's 77-year history (12 September 2001, against a non-state actor) = 0.013/yr, and never against the USSR or Russia despite Berlin 1948/1961, Cuba 1962, Able Archer 1983, the 2015 Turkish shootdown, and Przewodow 2022. Article 4 has been invoked eight times, including twice in September 2025 (Poland and Estonia) - allies have consistently chosen Article 4 precisely to avoid Article 5.
events.reasoning: The 3.0x multiplier is at the top of the doctrinally defensible band and reflects a real structural change: an active great-power war on the alliance border and a member state now firing on intruders. It should not go higher, because Article 5 is a discretionary political act requiring consensus among 32 governments, and the observed institutional response to every provocation since 2022 has been Article 4 plus a named operation (Eastern Sentry, Baltic Sentry), not Article 5. 0.013*3.0 = 0.039/yr. p_2027 = 1-exp(-0.039*1.4) = 0.053, shaded to 0.04 because a US administration actively drawing down 5,000 troops from Germany and cutting BCTs 4->3 is the least likely US government to consent. p_2030 = 1-exp(-[0.039*2.6 + 0.016*1.8]) = 0.12 -> 0.10. p_2036 = adds ~6 further years at ~0.016 -> cumulative 0.22 -> 0.15. Consistency check against nato_russia_direct_clash: this implies P(Article 5 | lethal clash) is roughly 0.33 near term and 0.39 by 2036, which is reasonable given that a single fatality in an air incident (Turkey 2015 precedent) would almost certainly not trigger it, whereas a deliberate ground or missile attack would.

events.statement: Vladimir Putin ceases to be Russia's paramount leader through death, resignation, incapacitation, or removal.
events.resolution_criteria: Putin is no longer President of the Russian Federation and is not exercising paramount power through another formal office, as confirmed by official Russian state announcement or by the sustained public exercise of presidential authority by another individual for 60+ consecutive days.
events.reference_class: Two components. (1) Actuarial: a male aged 73 (74 in Oct 2026) with elite medical care faces roughly 1.8-2.2% annual all-cause mortality, rising to ~5%/yr by 80 and ~8%/yr by 84. (2) Irregular exit: Geddes-Wright-Frantz autocratic-regimes data give consolidated personalist leaders with 20+ years in office an irregular-exit hazard of roughly 3-4%/yr (Mubarak 30y, Ben Ali 23y, Gaddafi 42y, Assad senior/junior, Nazarbayev, Lukashenko survived 2020). Combined ~5%/yr in 2026, rising with age.
events.reasoning: Only 1.15x uplift, because the visible indicators of elite fracture are absent: no faction has defected since Prigozhin's 2023 mutiny, the security services remain cohesive, there is no protest movement, and the CBR is cutting rates into 6% inflation rather than managing a collapse. Fiscal stress is real but the state has ~20% debt/GDP of borrowing room, raised VAT to 22% for 2026, and has been substituting OFZ issuance for NWF drawdown. Hazard ~0.057/yr in 2026, rising with age to ~0.075 by 2030 and ~0.11 by 2036. Cumulative hazard: to end-2027, 0.057*1.4 = 0.080 -> p 0.077 -> 0.07. To 2030, 0.057*1.4 + 0.068*3.0 = 0.284 -> p 0.247 -> 0.23. To 2036, add 6.4 further years averaging ~0.093 = 0.595, total 0.879 -> p 0.585, shaded to 0.54 to acknowledge that survivorship among long-tenured autocrats is systematically better than base tables imply (selection for exceptional health and exceptional security). Note this event is deliberately silent on the direction of any successor's policy; the impact vector encodes only the modal outcome of consolidation-plus-war-fatigue.

events.statement: A structural rupture in the EU: an Article 50 withdrawal notification, a lapse of EU sectoral sanctions on Russia through failure of unanimity, or suspension of a member state's Council voting rights under Article 7(3).
events.resolution_criteria: Any one of: (a) a member state formally notifies the European Council of its intention to withdraw under Article 50 TEU; (b) EU sectoral/economic sanctions on Russia lapse and remain lapsed for 30+ days because a renewal failed to achieve unanimity, in the absence of a comprehensive peace settlement that the Council has endorsed; (c) the Council determines under Article 7(3) to suspend a member state's voting rights.
events.reference_class: Article 50 notification: one in 68 years of the EEC/EU = 0.015/yr. Sanctions lapse: zero in 24 consecutive six-month renewal cycles since July 2014 (12 years), despite roughly five occasions on which Hungary held a renewal hostage for weeks. Article 7(3) suspension: never used in EU history (Article 7(1) opened against Poland 2017 and Hungary 2018, neither reaching suspension). Combined ~0.025/yr.
events.reasoning: This is the one place where 2026 news cuts strongly AGAINST the consensus narrative and the multiplier belongs below 1.0. Orban's defeat on 12 April 2026 removed the single veto player who had blocked sanctions renewals, joint debt and enlargement for a decade; the new Hungarian government has already ended the 17-month accession veto and let cluster 1 open on 15 June. The EU adopted its 21st sanctions package on 23 July with no lapse. Belgium's obstruction of the reparations loan is a legal-liability dispute resolved by borrowing €90bn instead, which is bargaining, not fracture. Against that, AfD sits at a record 28-29% with German eastern state elections in September, France is in budgetary paralysis, and RN leads the 2027 French field. Multiplier 0.85 -> 0.021/yr now, rising to ~0.035/yr after the 2027 French presidential election. p_2027 = 1-exp(-0.021*1.4) = 0.029 -> 0.03. p_2030 = 1-exp(-[0.021*1.4 + 0.033*3.0]) = 0.12 -> 0.11. p_2036 = adds 6.4 years at ~0.038 = 0.243 -> cumulative 0.372 -> p 0.31, shaded to 0.26 because the observed EU response to every prior shock (2015, 2016, 2020, 2022) has been deeper integration under stress, and because the sanctions-lapse leg is largely neutralised if a peace settlement arrives first (a settlement-driven unwinding does not resolve this YES).

events.statement: NATO's European allies plus Canada collectively reach at least 3.5% of GDP on core defence spending in a single calendar year.
events.resolution_criteria: NATO's official annual 'Defence Expenditure of NATO Countries' release reports aggregate core defence spending (the 3.5% pillar, excluding the 1.5% defence-related pillar) for European allies plus Canada at 3.50% of combined GDP or above for a given calendar year.
events.reference_class: Peacetime alliance rearmament rates. NATO Europe went 2.02% (2024) -> ~2.2% (2025) -> 2.53% (2026), i.e. ~0.25pp/yr, the fastest sustained European build-up since the early 1950s. Comparators: US 5.0%->9.3% of GDP in two years during Korea (wartime); NATO Europe declined from ~3.5% to 1.4% over 1990-2014 at -0.09pp/yr. The 2014 Wales 2% pledge took a full decade to reach in aggregate and was hit almost exactly on its 2024 deadline, with 9 of 32 allies still short.
events.reasoning: This is a threshold crossing on a trending series, not a Poisson shock, so the base rate is the implied annual crossing probability given the trajectory and the multiplier reflects the current unusually steep gradient. From 2.53% the gap is 0.97pp. p_2027 is near zero: no plausible one-year jump of ~1pp exists outside mobilisation, so 0.02. To reach 3.5% by 2030 requires sustaining 0.24pp/yr for four more years - exactly the current pace, but with the pace almost certain to decelerate as the easy money (munitions restocking, one-off procurement) is spent and as France, Italy, Spain and Belgium hit debt constraints; Spain has refused the 5% headline outright and Czechia, Hungary, Slovenia and the UK have made little progress. So 0.29, not 0.5. By 2036 the alliance's own deadline (2035) has passed, the US drawdown is a strong forcing function, and NATO aggregates have historically hit their targets roughly on schedule, but aggregate targets are met later than pledged more often than not: 0.62. Note the alliance has already booked >$139bn of added core investment since The Hague, which is the empirical anchor for the 0.25pp/yr gradient.

events.statement: A Russian-attributed sabotage or covert attack on NATO member territory kills at least five people and is publicly attributed to Russian state services by the victim government.
events.resolution_criteria: An incident on the territory of a NATO member (excluding declared combat operations) causing 5+ deaths, for which the government of that state publicly attributes responsibility to Russian state services (GRU, SVR, FSB or proxies directed by them). Deaths at sea aboard vessels of NATO-member flag count.
events.reference_class: The Russian sabotage campaign in Europe since 2022 has produced hundreds of incidents (arson, rail sabotage, parcel incendiaries, subsea cable cuts, GPS jamming) with zero mass-casualty outcomes. The nearest lethal precedent is Vrbetice, Czechia, October 2014: a GRU-attributed ammunition depot explosion that killed two, attributed publicly in April 2021. The July 2024 DHL parcel incendiaries were assessed as a near-miss for downing a cargo aircraft. So: zero 5+ fatality events in 12 years of the campaign; roughly one 2-fatality event.
events.reasoning: The incident count has risen roughly 7x since 2022 (10 -> ~70/yr) and the target set has escalated from warehouses to rail networks, aviation cargo and subsea power interconnectors, so a 2.3x multiplier on frequency is warranted. But the base rate must reflect that Russian tradecraft has deliberately calibrated *below* the mass-casualty line: these operations are meant to impose cost without triggering Article 5, and the operators are increasingly low-skill recruited proxies who produce less, not more, lethality. 0.035*2.3 = 0.08/yr while the war runs, ~0.04/yr after. p_2027 = 1-exp(-0.08*1.4) = 0.106 -> 0.10. p_2030 = 1-exp(-[0.08*2.6 + 0.045*1.8]) = 0.25. p_2036 = adds 6 years at ~0.04 -> cumulative 0.53 -> p 0.41, shaded to 0.37 for post-settlement decay. Confidence low because attribution practice is itself the binding constraint: governments have repeatedly declined to attribute publicly (the Baltic cable cuts were mostly resolved as 'anchor dragging'), so the resolution criterion can fail even when the underlying act occurs.

events.statement: The United States announces withdrawal from NATO's integrated military command structure, or US military personnel in Europe fall below 50,000.
events.resolution_criteria: Either (a) an official US announcement of withdrawal from NATO's integrated command structure or from the Treaty under Article 13, or (b) DoD/USEUCOM-reported total US military personnel in Europe (permanent plus rotational) below 50,000 for two consecutive quarterly reports.
events.reference_class: US troops in Europe: ~400k (1960s) -> 213k (1991) -> 63k trough (2013-2020) -> ~100-105k (2022) -> ~72k (2026). Major post-Cold-War drawdown decisions cutting >20% of theatre strength: roughly four in 35 years = 0.11/yr, but no US administration has ever taken the figure below ~60k, and the 2020 Trump order to cut 12,000 from Germany was reversed in 2021. Withdrawal from integrated command: France 1966; the US never, in 77 years.
events.reasoning: 2.0x is justified by an active, already-executing posture review rather than by rhetoric: Hegseth has cut theatre fighters 150->100, tankers by 8, ISR aircraft 26->15, BCTs 4->3, cancelled a 4,000-strong Poland/Romania rotation and is pulling ~5,000 from Germany, with the stated goal of returning to pre-2022 levels. But pre-2022 levels were ~63-65k, not below 50k; getting under 50k requires an additional decision beyond anything announced, and NDAA floor provisions plus bipartisan congressional resistance (GOP leaders publicly objected to the Romania cut) are real friction. Integrated-command withdrawal is a near-tail event even under this administration. 0.06*2.0 = 0.12/yr through Jan 2029, then ~0.05/yr under an unknown successor. p_2027 = 1-exp(-0.12*1.4) = 0.153, shaded to 0.12 because the announced trajectory lands at ~65k, not <50k. p_2030 = 1-exp(-[0.12*2.5 + 0.05*1.9]) = 0.33 -> 0.28. p_2036 = adds 6 years at ~0.045 -> cumulative 0.66 -> p 0.48, shaded to 0.41 since European rearmament reaching 3%+ would reduce, not increase, the pressure for a rupture-level cut once burden-sharing complaints are satisfied.

events.statement: Non-electoral regime change in Belarus or Moldova, or Russian/Russian-backed armed escalation in Moldova producing 100+ deaths.
events.resolution_criteria: Any of: (a) the head of state of Belarus or Moldova is replaced by means other than a scheduled election or constitutional succession following natural death (i.e. coup, revolution, forced resignation under duress, foreign-imposed change); (b) armed conflict involving Transnistrian, Russian or Moldovan forces on Moldovan territory causes 100+ battle deaths within 12 months per ACLED/UCDP.
events.reference_class: Post-Soviet non-electoral regime changes 1991-2026: Georgia 2003, Ukraine 2004 and 2014, Kyrgyzstan 2005, 2010 and 2020, Armenia 2018 - seven successes across twelve post-Soviet states in 35 years, i.e. ~0.017/state/yr, so ~0.033/yr for this two-state set; failed attempts (Belarus 2020, Kazakhstan 2022) are excluded. Armed conflict on Moldovan soil: once in 34 years (Transnistria 1992) = 0.029/yr. Combined ~0.05/yr.
events.reasoning: Only 1.2x. The dominant driver over the full horizon is actuarial rather than revolutionary: Lukashenko turns 72 in 2026 and will be 82 by 2036, and his exit would very likely be contested. Against escalation: Russia has no land corridor to Transnistria and cannot project force there while the Dnepr grouping is halted at Orikhiv; the Transnistrian entity is energy-starved and dependent on Chisinau's tolerance since the January 2025 gas cut-off; Moldova's pro-EU government consolidated its position in September 2025 and opened accession cluster 1 on 15 June 2026. For escalation: Russian electoral interference in the region is intense and rising, Belarus now hosts Oreshnik and rehearsed non-strategic nuclear employment with Russia in May 2026. 0.05*1.2 = 0.06/yr. p_2027 = 1-exp(-0.06*1.4) = 0.081 -> 0.08. p_2030 = 1-exp(-0.06*4.4) = 0.23 -> 0.22. p_2036 = 1-exp(-0.06*10.4) = 0.46, shaded to 0.40 because a constitutional succession on Lukashenko's death would not by itself resolve YES.

events.statement: Volodymyr Zelensky ceases to hold the office of President of Ukraine.
events.resolution_criteria: Zelensky is no longer President of Ukraine, whether through electoral defeat, resignation, impeachment, incapacity or death, confirmed by the inauguration or formal assumption of duties by a successor (including an acting president under Article 112 of the Ukrainian Constitution).
events.reference_class: Ukrainian presidential turnover: six presidents in 34 years, mean tenure 5.7 years = 0.18/yr, and no Ukrainian incumbent has ever won a second consecutive term (Kravchuk lost, Yushchenko lost, Yanukovych ousted, Poroshenko lost; only Kuchma served two full terms). Wartime leaders under martial law with suspended elections have much lower hazard (Churchill 1940-45, Ben-Gurion, Assad), roughly 0.06/yr. Zelensky is 7 years into office with elections constitutionally barred while martial law holds.
events.reasoning: The hazard is dominated by the ceasefire pathway: martial law bars elections, so once a durable ceasefire arrives, elections follow within roughly 60-90 days of martial law lapsing, and the Ukrainian base rate for incumbents is close to zero re-election. Adding the NABU energy-corruption scandal, which has already cost two ministers and the presidential chief of staff, drew charges against six more people on 12 May 2026, has now extended into banking and defence procurement, and reportedly touches Zelensky personally for the first time. Multiplier 1.25 -> 0.163/yr. p_2027 = 1-exp(-0.163*1.4) = 0.204 -> 0.18 (shaded down because no election can be held before a ceasefire and the war is more likely than not still running at end-2027). p_2030 = 1-exp(-0.163*4.4) = 0.51 -> 0.47. p_2036 = 1-exp(-0.16*10.4) = 0.81; nudged to 0.86 because 17 years in office would be an extreme outlier for any Ukrainian politician and because post-war elections are close to certain within the horizon.

events.statement: Russia enters acute fiscal or monetary distress: NWF liquid assets below $10bn, a domestic sovereign debt default or forced restructuring, or annual CPI inflation above 20%.
events.resolution_criteria: Any of: (a) Russian Ministry of Finance reports National Wealth Fund liquid assets below USD 10bn at month-end; (b) a missed payment or compulsory restructuring of rouble-denominated federal debt (OFZ); (c) Rosstat annual CPI above 20.0% year-on-year for any month.
events.reference_class: Russian fiscal/currency crises since 1991: 1992 hyperinflation, 1998 default and devaluation, 2014-15 rouble crisis, 2022 capital-control emergency - roughly three severe and two partial episodes in 34 years, i.e. ~0.09/yr for a crisis of this magnitude.
events.reasoning: 1.9x, and most of the probability mass sits in the mechanical NWF leg rather than in default or hyperinflation. Arithmetic: liquid NWF is $35.7bn and the Jan-Apr 2026 deficit alone was $78.4bn against a $50.5bn full-year plan, with hydrocarbon revenue down 38.3% y/y, Urals at $54 against a $59 budget assumption, and 42.7% of refining capacity disabled by Ukrainian strikes. At the Jan-Feb 2026 record drawdown pace the fund would be exhausted inside two years. Countervailing and the reason the multiplier is not higher: MinFin has been substituting OFZ issuance for NWF sales, public debt is only ~20% of GDP, VAT was raised to 22% for 2026, inflation is falling (6.0% in June against a 6-7% CBR range) and the CBR is cutting rather than defending, so legs (b) and (c) are remote. 0.09*1.9 = 0.171/yr near term. p_2027 = 1-exp(-0.171*1.4) = 0.212 -> 0.21. p_2030 = declining hazard as oil mean-reverts toward $60 and the war likely ends: average ~0.135 over 4.4 years -> 1-exp(-0.594) = 0.45. p_2036 = adds 6 years at ~0.055 -> cumulative 0.92 -> p 0.60.

events.statement: NATO-member ground forces deploy inside Ukraine in a formation of at least 1,000 personnel under a national or multinational reassurance mandate.
events.resolution_criteria: At least 1,000 uniformed personnel of one or more NATO member states officially present on Ukrainian government-controlled territory under an announced reassurance, monitoring or training mandate, confirmed by the contributing government(s). Excludes embassy security, existing small training/liaison detachments and private contractors.
events.reference_class: Third-party ground deployments following interstate ceasefires since 1990: monitoring or peacekeeping forces were deployed after roughly half of ceasefires in interstate wars, but NATO-member national forces entering the territory of a non-member adjacent to a nuclear-armed adversary has no direct precedent. The 'Coalition of the Willing' has been planning such a force since March 2025 without deploying, through 16 months of stalled diplomacy.
events.reasoning: This is close to a pure conditional on ukraine_durable_ceasefire, since no European government will insert a brigade-sized force into an active war. Conditional probability of deployment given a durable ceasefire: roughly 0.5 - the coalition has done the planning and the UK, France and the Baltics are committed in principle, but Russia has made exclusion of NATO troops a core demand in the Geneva track, any US-brokered settlement is likely to constrain it, and the US has declined to provide the enabling backstop the coalition said it required. Applying 0.5 to the ceasefire path: p_2027 = 0.5*0.16 = 0.08; p_2030 = 0.5*0.49 = 0.245 -> 0.25; p_2036 = 0.5*0.79 = 0.395, plus a small unconditional residual for a pre-ceasefire western-Ukraine air-defence or training deployment -> 0.41.

couplings.mechanism: Combat intensity near the border directly generates the spillover events that drive tension: drone and missile debris into Romania and Poland, air-policing scrambles, Article 4 requests. Romania's 7 violations in four months tracked the tempo of Russian strikes on Danube ports.

Nearly all NATO airspace violations in 2025-26 are Shahed-type drones straying or being routed along the Danube and Black Sea coast during mass strike packages. Violation counts are close to a linear function of monthly one-way attack drone launches.

Casualties are a constituent of the intensity composite; the residual coupling reflects the assault-tempo channel, where Russian infantry losses scale with the number of small-group assaults ordered per week.
Each violation cluster produces summonses of Russian envoys, Article 4 consultations and reinforcement of Eastern Sentry, which are the observable components of the tension index.

Threat perception drives budget appropriations with a lag set by national budget cycles: the Sept 2025 Poland/Estonia incursions fed into 2026 budgets, and the >$139bn of added core investment since The Hague was legislated through 2026 finance acts.

Reflexive escalation: Moscow calibrates sabotage tempo to signal cost against arms transfers and asset seizure, so hybrid activity rises with the adversarial temperature rather than being independent of it.

Subsea cable and rail sabotage translates into resilience, counter-drone and maritime-surveillance line items, and is the main political driver of the 1.5% defence-related pillar of the 5% NATO commitment.

Substitution: US drawdown announcements (fighters 150->100, BCTs 4->3, 5,000 out of Germany) are the single most cited justification in 2026 European defence budget debates. Falling US presence raises European spending with a budget-cycle lag.

Weak negative: reduced US presence lowers the density of NATO-Russia contact but raises Russian probing incentives on the eastern flank. Net effect is small and sign-ambiguous; modelled as slightly tension-raising when troops fall.

Oil and gas supplied ~30% of federal revenue before 2026 and fell 38.3% y/y in Jan-Apr when Urals traded near $50 against a $59 budget assumption. The mineral extraction tax and export duty are near-linear in the Urals price with a one-to-two-quarter collection lag.
Oil price is the dominant single input to the stress composite through the fiscal, current-account and rouble channels simultaneously.
The NWF is the residual financing source after OFZ issuance. The Jan-Feb 2026 record RUB 12.8bn/day of yuan and gold sales was a direct function of the early-year revenue shortfall.
Deficit/GDP is a direct component of the stress composite and drives the borrowing, taxation and money-creation responses that generate the rest of it.
A high policy rate suppresses civilian investment and raises the fiscal cost of subsidised lending programmes, which is why the CBR has been cutting (21% -> 14%) despite fiscal pressure.

Fiscal constraint eventually bites on recruitment bonuses and munitions procurement. The effect is small and slow: Russia has cut civilian spending rather than defence, and 2025 MoD outlays still reached 7.3% of GDP.

Recruitment is bought with signing bonuses funded by regional and federal budgets; fiscal stress cuts bonus levels, which has already shown up as daily recruitment falling from a 1,100-1,150 target to ~940 and losses exceeding intake since Dec 2025.

Fragmented national parliaments produce weak or veto-prone governments in the Council; the AfD at 28-29% and France's budgetary paralysis directly constrain what Berlin and Paris can commit to at EU level.
Coalition instability delays multi-year procurement programmes and makes debt-financed defence packages harder to legislate. France's failure to pass a 2026 budget is the clearest current instance.

With US direct appropriations at zero, Ukraine's financing runs through unanimity-dependent EU instruments: the €90bn 2026-27 loan needed a Council decision, and the reparations loan died on Belgian objection.
Interceptor and artillery supply determines whether Ukraine can hold the Kramatorsk-Kostiantynivka belt. Supply gaps in mid-2024 and late-2025 preceded the fastest Russian gains of the war.
More materiel raises both sides' expenditure of fires and sustains the deep-strike campaign, raising measured intensity even when the line is static.

Ukrainian deep strikes on refineries and Baltic/Black Sea export terminals tighten Russian product markets and occasionally the global crude balance; the campaign that disabled 42.7% of refining capacity cut ~500 kb/d of runs, pushing some crude to export at a wider discount but supporting outright price.

Cross-domain. Urals is mechanically Brent minus a sanctions/logistics discount that has ranged from $2 to $20 and stood at ~$7 at Indian ports on 1 July 2026. The price cap at $44.10 binds only on G7-serviced cargoes.

Cross-domain. US theatre posture in Europe is set by the National Defense Strategy and administration preference, not by threat assessment: the 2026 drawdown was ordered while Russian airspace violations were at record levels.
Cross-domain. Chinese and Indian crude purchases, yuan settlement and dual-use component flows are the marginal determinant of whether US SDN designations on Rosneft and Lukoil actually bind.
Cross-domain. The 2026 Iran war episode pushed Russian crude to a premium earlier in the year before Asian demand weakened; it also diverted US mediation bandwidth away from the Ukraine track.

key_uncertainties: Whether the July 2026 'air ceasefire' proposal is a genuine stepping stone to a general ceasefire or a face-saving device that freezes diplomacy at a partial measure. A domain-limited truce would not resolve ukraine_durable_ceasefire but would sharply cut measured conflict intensity, decoupling the two variables the model normally treats as tied.

Ukraine's infantry sustainability. The 850k end-2026 force target, 165,200 AWOL cases in ten months of 2025 and stalled mobilisation reform make a non-linear line collapse the single largest fat tail on the Ukrainian side - and it would not be preceded by the gradual territorial signals the model uses as a leading indicator.

Whether Russia's fiscal position degrades gradually or discontinuously. NWF liquid assets of $35.7bn against a Jan-Apr deficit of $78.4bn imply exhaustion within two years at the early-2026 pace, but OFZ substitution, the VAT rise to 22% and any oil recovery could stretch it indefinitely. The model cannot distinguish 'running out of money' from 'choosing to borrow instead'.

Attribution practice for hybrid attacks. Several Baltic cable incidents were officially resolved as accidents. If governments continue to under-attribute in order to avoid escalation obligations, russia_lethal_hybrid_attack_nato can fail to resolve even when the underlying act occurs, and the hybrid incident count is a systematic undercount of true activity.

The durability of the European rearmament gradient. The 0.25pp/yr pace since 2024 has been driven by one-off restocking and by countries already above 3%; France, Italy, Spain and Belgium face debt constraints, and Spain has refused the 5% headline. Whether the curve is linear or logistic determines european_rearmament_milestone almost entirely.

Direction of Russian policy after a leadership transition. The model encodes a modal de-escalation, but the successor pool (Dyumin, Patrushev fils) comes from the security services and a consolidation-through-escalation path is roughly as plausible as a settlement path. Treat the sign of that impact vector as genuinely uncertain.

Whether Hungary's post-Orban government converts into durable EU cohesion. Budapest lifted the accession veto in June 2026 but still blocked clusters 2-3 on 22 July, which suggests national-interest obstruction persists independent of Orban and that the eu_cohesion_index improvement may be smaller than the election result implies.

US force posture floor. Congressional NDAA provisions and GOP resistance to the Romania cut may impose a hard floor well above 50,000, in which case us_nato_commitment_rupture is materially overstated. Conversely, a peace settlement would remove the political justification for any floor at all.

Whether European reassurance troops in Ukraine are a settlement enabler or a settlement blocker. Russia has made their exclusion a core Geneva demand, so the same variable that raises Ukraine's willingness to sign lowers Russia's, and the model's treatment of european_troops_deployed_ukraine as downstream of a ceasefire may invert.
surprises_2026: 12 April 2026: Viktor Orban lost the Hungarian election after 16 years. Peter Magyar's Tisza took 53.6% and 138 of 199 seats - a constitutional two-thirds supermajority - against Fidesz's 37.8% and 55 seats, on ~80% turnout and 3.3m votes, the largest ever for a Hungarian party. Orban conceded on the night. This removes the EU's single most consistent veto player on sanctions, joint debt and enlargement.

June 2026: the new Hungarian government ended Budapest's 17-month veto on Ukraine's EU accession, and cluster 1 ('Fundamentals') opened for both Ukraine and Moldova on 15 June. Hungary nonetheless continued to block clusters 2 and 3 on 22 July, pushing the next attempt to 1 September - obstruction survived the change of government.

February-March 2026: Ukraine ran a successful local counteroffensive on the 'Oleksandrivka front' in eastern Dnipropetrovsk, reclaiming 300-400 km2 and eight settlements, effectively clearing the oblast and halting Russia's Dnepr grouping near Orikhiv. This is the first meaningful Ukrainian territorial reversal since 2022 and inverts the assumption of monotonic Russian advance.

The Russian advance rate has collapsed to near zero: net gains of 5 sq mi (ISW) to 15 sq mi (DeepState) in the four weeks to 14 July 2026, against 10 sq mi in the preceding four weeks - the slowest sustained rate of the war, despite Russia having taken Pokrovsk and Myrnohrad in early 2026.

Russia's monthly losses have exceeded its recruitment for every month since December 2025: 30,000-34,000 casualties per month against ~27,000 recruits, with actual daily sign-ups at ~940 against a 1,100-1,150 target. March 2026 set a single-month casualty record of 35,000. Cumulative Russian casualties reached ~1.4 million with 400,000-450,000 fatalities by June 2026.

Ukraine's deep-strike campaign has hit all ten of Russia's largest refineries during 2026 (11 refineries in June alone), disabling 42.7% of projected refining capacity as of early July and cutting ~500 kb/d of crude runs. Cumulative refining-sector losses of ~$13.5bn since August 2025, with fuel rationing and export restrictions inside Russia.

Russian fiscal deterioration is far worse than the 2026 budget assumed: the Jan-Apr 2026 deficit alone was $78.4bn against a $50.5bn full-year plan, hydrocarbon revenue fell 38.3% y/y to $30.6bn, Urals averaged ~$39 in December 2025 against a $59 budget assumption, and NWF liquid assets are down to $35.7bn from $185bn in 2021. MinFin ran record daily FX/gold sales of RUB 12.8bn/day from 16 Jan to 5 Feb 2026.

The Bank of Russia has been easing aggressively into the fiscal crisis rather than tightening: key rate cut to 14.00% on 24 July 2026 (from 21% peak, via 15% and 14.5% in April), with CPI at 6.0% in June and the 2026 GDP forecast cut to 0.0-1.0% in July from 0.5-1.5% in April.

NATO's Ankara summit, 7-8 July 2026, produced a declaration naming Russia a threat to Euro-Atlantic security, a €70bn military aid pledge for Ukraine in 2026 with equivalent intent for 2027, and language stating that 'Ukraine contributes to transatlantic security'. Allies logged >$139bn of added European and Canadian core defence investment since The Hague 2025.

European allies plus Canada reached 2.53% of GDP (~$634bn) on defence in 2026, up from 2.02% in 2024 - a 0.25pp/yr gradient. EU-27 spending alone hit €454bn (2.4% of EU GDP) from €418bn in 2025. Lithuania 5.33%, Estonia 5.1%, Latvia 4.92%. The Council activated the national escape clause for 18 member states by February 2026.

Simultaneously, the US executed a substantial drawdown: theatre fighters cut 150->100, eight tankers withdrawn, ISR aircraft 26->15, brigade combat teams 4->3, a planned 4,000-strong rotation to Poland and Romania cancelled outright, ~5,000 troops leaving Germany over 6-12 months, and only ~1,000 US soldiers left in Romania. GOP congressional leaders publicly objected.

Romania became the first NATO state to routinely engage intruders, shooting down drones on three consecutive days in late July 2026 after logging 7 airspace violations, 11 munition-fragment finds and 18 air-policing scrambles by 28 April. NATO jets shot down a drone over Latvia on 8 June 2026.

The AfD reached a record 28-29% in July 2026 polling (Insa 29%, Ipsos 28%, PolitPro trend 27.7%) with an 8.5-point lead over Merz's CDU/CSU at ~22% - the largest lead Insa has ever recorded - ahead of eastern German state elections in September 2026. Merz's coalition agreed a reform package with €10bn in annual income tax relief on 1-2 July.

The EU's reparations loan using €210bn of immobilised Russian assets failed on Belgian objection in December 2025; leaders instead agreed a €90bn 2026-27 loan financed by EU market borrowing against the EU budget, repayable by Ukraine only once it receives reparations. The Commission is now seeking an additional €25bn tranche.

The EU adopted its 21st sanctions package on 23 July 2026, freezing the Russian crude price cap at $44.10/bbl for a year and suspending the dynamic mechanism adopted in January 2026, while carving out LNG transfer allowances and adding the most listings in four years.

Two short truces occurred and both collapsed: a 32-hour Orthodox Easter truce from 13:00 UTC on 11 April 2026, and a 9-11 May Victory Day truce with a prisoner exchange. Both were humanitarian pauses, not settlements, with mutual violation accusations.

US mediation stalled and was partially displaced by an Iran war in 2026. A US-set June deadline for a peace deal lapsed; Zelensky's 4 June public letter proposing a leaders' meeting in a third country was rebuffed by Putin, who insisted on full Russian control of Donbas as a precondition. The Geneva trilateral of 17-18 February 2026 was the first round to put territory formally on the agenda.

Trump publicly disclaimed US arms transfers to Ukraine on 24-25 July 2026, stating he sells weapons only to NATO countries and has 'no idea' how they are distributed - formalising PURL as a European-funded procurement channel with zero direct US appropriation.

Ukraine's NABU energy-procurement scandal expanded through 2026: two ministers and the presidential chief of staff were dismissed, money-laundering charges were pressed against six more people on 12 May 2026, and the case has since extended into banking and defence procurement, with reporting that evidence may for the first time implicate Zelensky personally.

Russia and Belarus conducted an unannounced joint nuclear exercise in May 2026 including Belarusian launch sites, with Lukashenko visiting a missile brigade; Belarus has hosted the Oreshnik IRBM since 2025 and rehearsed non-strategic nuclear employment 'from unprepared positions'.

Armenia held parliamentary elections on 7 June 2026 which Pashinyan characterises as having given the Azerbaijan peace 'legitimacy'. The treaty remains initialled but unsigned pending Armenian constitutional amendment; the US-managed TRIPP corridor under a 99-year lease has displaced Russia's Article 9 role from the 2020 trilateral statement. Rubio signed a US-Armenia strategic partnership in May 2026.
